text:
Droit de la famille — 17338

2017 QCCS 679

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-04-059037-128

DATE:

February 23, 2017

______________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

CHANTAL TREMBLAY, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

D. M.

Plaintiff

v.

J. L.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

1.      OVERVIEW

[
1
]

Plaintiff requests shared custody of the
parties’ seven years old child and to adjust child support accordingly.

[
2
]

Defendant contests the request and asks the
Court to maintain the status quo. Alternatively, she requests progressive
shared custody to be exercised on a 2-2-3 or 3‑1-3 day basis provided
that the child adjusts well to the new custody measures and that custody
modalities are implemented through play therapy. She also asks for the inclusion
of expenses relating to camps and other activities in the basic parental
contribution for child support as well as the reimbursement of special
expenses.

2.       CONTEXT

[
3
]

The parties lived together for approximately
three years from 2007 to 2010. They are the parents of X, born on [...], 2009.
He is presently 7 years old.

[
4
]

On September 10, 2012, the parties signed an
agreement regarding custody and child support.

[
5
]

On November 25, 2015, Plaintiff filed a Motion
for shared custody.

[
6
]

On January 15, 2016, the parties signed an
interim agreement modifying the child support payable to Defendant.

[
7
]

On October 26, 2016, Defendant filed a Motion
for progressive shared custody, child support, and reimbursement of special
expenses in proportion of the parties’ respective revenues.

[
8
]

On November 28, 2016, both motions were heard on
the merits.

[
9
]

On December 2, 2016, Defendant filed a Motion
for a reopening of the hearing.

[
10
]

On December 15, 2016, the Court allowed
Defendant and her new partner to testify in light of the allegations concerning
the child’s safety. The Court heard this new evidence under reserve of
Plaintiff’s rights to respond to these new allegations. Plaintiff’s attorney
cross-examined the witnesses on that same day and confirmed that she does not
have further evidence to present.

[
11
]

On December 20, 2016, Defendant amended her
Motion seeking to maintain the status quo as she is no longer comfortable with
progressive shared custody.

3.       DISCUSSION

3.1     Custody of the child

3.1.1   Significant change

[
12
]

The Court may review decisions concerning a
child at any time, if warranted by circumstances.
[1]

[
13
]

Before a Court renders a
variation order in respect of a custody order, it must be satisfied that there
has been a change in the condition, means, needs, or other circumstances of the
child since the custody order was rendered.

[
14
]

On September 19, 2012, the Court homologated the
parties’ agreement concerning custody and child support. At that time, X was
three years old.

[
15
]

Defendant was granted custody of X with the
following visitation rights for Plaintiff as of October 15, 2012:

Week 1: Wednesday at 5:00 pm until Friday 9:00 am;

Week 2: Monday at 5:00 pm until 7:30 pm and Friday at
5:00 pm until Sunday at 7:30 pm.

[
16
]

At the time of this agreement, Plaintiff was
working full time at [Company A], and Defendant was unemployed. Defendant lived
in the family residence in Town A until December 2012 and then moved out with
the child to live at her sister’s duplex in Town B. Plaintiff later sold the
family residence and bought a condominium in Town A.

[
17
]

Defendant started working part time in September
2014 and full time as of March 2015. She is unemployed since May 2016. She
lives with a new partner and his three boys since June 2016. His children are
on a 2-2-3 day custody schedule.

[
18
]

Plaintiff explains that, in 2012, he agreed that
Defendant be granted custody of X as the child was still very young. He now
requests shared custody because the child is older and wishes to spend more
time with him. In May 2016, in light of his request for shared custody,
Plaintiff moved to Town B with his fiancée and rented his condominium in Town A.
Plaintiff’s new residence is less than a five-minute walk from the child’s
school A.

[
19
]

Defendant admits that X expressed the need to
see his father more often, but she claims that he has now changed his mind.
According to her, X also expressed concerns with not seeing his mother on a
regular basis.

[
20
]

In light of the above, the Court is satisfied
that, since 2012, there have been significant changes in the child’s needs,
means, and conditions. Therefore, the Court considers that a review of the
custody agreement is justified.

3.1.2   Request for shared
custody

[
21
]

When analyzing a request for shared custody, the
Court considers the following criteria
[2]
:

a)         the child’s age, needs, and desires;

b)         the parents’ ability to attend to the child’s development
and well-being;

c)         each parent’s educational, moral, and spiritual values;

d)         each parent’s ability to provide a stable environment for
the child;

e)         each parent’s availabilities to devote time and resources
to the child’s well-being;

f)          the parents’ communication ability;

g)         the proximity of the parents’ residences;

h)        the absence of parental alienation and each parent’s understanding
of the importance of maintaining contact with the other parent.

[
22
]

Plaintiff requests shared custody of the child
on a weekly alternating schedule. He believes that such an arrangement would be
in the child’s best interests as it would minimize the stress in the child’s
life and avoid disrupting the child’s routine.

[
23
]

In her initial Motion, Defendant requested that
shared custody be exercised on a 2-2-3 or 3-1-3 day basis provided that X
adjusts well to the new custody measures and that custody modalities are
implemented through play therapy.

[
24
]

However, in light of recent developments, she
now claims that Plaintiff does not provide X with a safe and healthy environment.
Therefore, she is no longer comfortable with progressive shared custody and
asks the Court to maintain the status quo.

[
25
]

Defendant’s Motion for reopening the hearing is
based on a discussion that occurred outside the court room at the end of the
hearing on November 28, 2016. Defendant learned that her partner’s ex-wife
provided information to Plaintiff in view of this hearing.

[
26
]

At the reopening of the hearing on December 15,
2016, Defendant explained that a complaint for harassment was filed against her
partner’s ex-wife and that they had to install cameras at their residence.
Defendant informed Plaintiff of this situation only after the hearing on
November 28, 2016, but Plaintiff responded that he was free to speak with
whomever he wants. Therefore, Defendant now has serious concerns regarding
shared custody. She views Plaintiff’s conduct as permitting the intrusion of a
third party in X’ life without consideration for the harm that this may cause
to X.

[
27
]

The Court considers that this new evidence does
not interfere with Plaintiff’s ability to provide a safe environment for X.
Therefore, this new evidence will have no bearing on the determination of
Plaintiff’s request for shared custody.

[
28
]

Since May 2016, Plaintiff now lives in a six and
a half apartment in Town B with his fiancé who he met back in 2012. X has a
very good relationship with both his father and his father’s fiancé.

[
29
]

Defendant is with her new partner since March
2015. The latter has three young boys
[3]
with a 2-2-3 day custody arrangement. Defendant and her partner
moved in together in June 2016.

[
30
]

The Court cannot accept Defendant’s testimony
regarding the potential impacts of new custody measures on X. On one hand, she
affirms that X had no difficulties adjusting to the new environment with her
partner and his three children. On the other hand, she claims that X would have
difficulties adjusting to new custody measures with his father due to his
anxiety problem. She also believes that a weekly alternating schedule would add
stress to X’ life since he expressed in the past concerns about his mother
abandoning him.

[
31
]

The evidence showed that X’ anxiety issues are
occasional. Defendant referred to four incidents of breathing, coughing, or
facial tics. The first incident occurred after X’ first sleep over at his
father’s residence at the age of two and a half. The second one occurred after
the sale of the family residence. The third incident relates to X not seeing
his father for a prolonged period of three months. The last one coincides with
Defendant’s partner and his three children moving in. However, Defendant
believes that the cause of the last incident relates rather to comments made by
Plaintiff about her.

[
32
]

Furthermore, X is already separated from his
mother for one week out of two during the winter holidays. Similarly, during
the summer period, X is with each parent for two non-consecutive weeks. The
parties did not raise any adaptation difficulties during those periods, and
they both request to keep these same arrangements going forward. The Court does
not see why this situation would be any different during the school year.

[
33
]

Considering that both parents are capable of
taking good care of X, the Court does not consider the child’s anxiety problem
as an obstacle for ordering shared custody. Furthermore, the fact that
Defendant refuses shared custody or that the parties have some difficulties
communicating with each other does not prohibit shared custody.
[4]

[
34
]

The Court concludes that Defendant did not
demonstrate the need for progressive shared custody or play therapy and that it
is in X’ best interests to order shared custody. The Court considers that
shared custody shall be established on a weekly alternating schedule to avoid
disrupting X’ routine with school and his other activities.

[
35
]

Defendant also requests to spend important
Jewish holidays
[5]
with
X and that the following modalities be incorporated in the custody judgment:

i)

winter holidays shall be split in two, one week
with each parent;

ii)

spring break vacation shall be split in two. The
parent not being able to take time off work shall offer to the other parent the
opportunity to have custody during the day;

iii)

X shall spend the day with Defendant on her
birthday and with Plaintiff on his birthday;

iv)

X shall spend his birthday with Defendant on odd
years and with Plaintiff on even years;

v)

each parent shall have the child for a maximum
of two non-consecutive weeks of vacation time per year, unless both parents
agree to a longer period. Vacation schedules shall not interfere with the
rotating schedule which will be picked up where it ended before each break;

vi)

the parties shall have to sign all documents
necessary to enable the minor child to leave Canada with the other parent for a
vacation provided there is mutual consent. The travelling parent shall give an
advance written notice  15 days before each vacation to the other parent with
the full disclosure of the itinerary and provide the other parent with easy
access to the child by phone during the vacation period; the child shall be
accompanied either by a parent or by an adult that the child is familiar with
and who has been agreed upon by both parents;

vii)

parties shall use an online co-parenting tool to
facilitate communication regarding X’ needs.

[
36
]

Plaintiff agrees with Defendant’s additional
modalities except for the following caveats:

1)

he wants the court to limit the number of days
the child will spend with Defendant for the Jewish holidays when they last more
than two days (ex: Passover and Hanouka last eight days);

2)

when Jewish and Christian holidays conflict (ex:
Christmas and Easter), he asks to have priority in view of the fact that there
are more Jewish holidays in a given year.

[
37
]

The Court endorses the custody modalities agreed
by the parties.  As for Jewish holidays, the Court maintains the modalities of the
2012 agreement. The child will be with Defendant for all important Jewish holidays,
[6]
but
if these holidays fall on Plaintiff’s time, the parties shall exchange those
days, when possible. Furthermore, the child shall be with his father on
Christmas Eve and Easter unless the parties agree otherwise.

4.2     Child support and special expenses

[
38
]

Article 587.2

C.c.Q.
states that a parent must contribute
to the basic parental contribution and special expenses related to his
child:

The support to be provided by a
parent for his child is equal to that parent’s share of the basic parental
contribution, increased, where applicable, having regard to specified expenses
relating to the child.

(…)

[
39
]

The expenses are considered special expenses
when they exceed the basic needs included in the child support. These basic
needs concern food, housing, communication, housekeeping, personal care,
clothing, furnishing, transport, and leisure.
[7]

[
40
]

The Court of Appeal
[8]

deals with the admissibility of special expenses in these terms:

Les
articles 587.1
alinéa 2
C.c.Q.

et l’article 9 du
Règlement sur la fixation des pensions alimentaires pour
enfant
imposent une double limite à l’admissibilité des frais particuliers;
en premier lieu, ils doivent être raisonnables eu égard aux besoins et aux
facultés des parents et, en deuxième lieu, ils doivent être liés aux besoins
dictés par la situation particulière de l’enfant.

4.2.1    Basic child
support including activities and camp fees

[
41
]

Defendant requests to include in the basic
parental contribution an amount of $1,500 for activities and $2,080 for camps.

[
42
]

Plaintiff contests this request since Defendant
has never solicited his opinion or advice in selecting activities or summer
camps.

[
43
]

The Court considers that activities and camp
fees shall be dealt with as special expenses since Defendant did not
demonstrate that these fees are recurrent or that both parents agreed on these
amounts based on the child’s particular needs.

[
44
]

Both parties agree that Plaintiff’s revenues
amount to $84,556.00 for the establishment of child support. In order to avoid
having to modify the child support amount in the near future, Plaintiff does
not want Defendant’s employment insurance benefits to be included in the
computation of child support.

[
45
]

In light of the above, the Court establishes
child support at a monthly amount of $382.02.

4.2.2    Special expenses

[
46
]

Defendant claims special expenses, which include
medical expenses, school fees, camp fees, and activities, for a total amount of
$8,515.16.

Medical expenses

[
47
]

Defendant claims medical expenses for
vaccinations administered to the child since his birth for a total amount of
$2,345. She filed a note dated January 26, 2016 from the child’s pediatrician
listing the vaccinations administered in his office and the related charges.
However, this list does not specify when the vaccinations were administered.
Moreover, Defendant did not file any proof of payment.

[
48
]

Plaintiff refuses to reimburse these
vaccinations for the following reasons:

i-

18 out of the 20 vaccinations listed were
administered prior to December 2011;

ii-

8 of the vaccinations were administered and paid
for prior to the parties’ separation in 2010;

iii-

he already paid for these expenses with the
exception of two vaccinations;

iv-

Defendant is claiming tax deduction for expenses
disbursed by him despite a provision in the 2012 agreement that he would be the
sole party able to deduct these expenses in his income tax report. Defendant
received a $597.51 refund on her 2015 federal income tax return and $394.70 on
her provincial income tax return for a total credit of $992.21 relating to
vaccinations;

v-

these vaccinations are provided free of charge
through the Quebec Immunisation Program.

[
49
]

Plaintiff requests a Court order that the
payments for medical and dental expenses be managed and paid by him directly
with the service provider. He also asks that receipts be remitted to him for
insurance claim purposes. Finally, he asks that Defendant refund him the
portion of these expenses not covered in proportion of her earnings.

[
50
]

Defendant agrees that Plaintiff pay directly the
service provider.

[
51
]

The Court dismisses Defendant’s claim for the
vaccination expenses as she did not demonstrate when these vaccinations were
administered or who paid for them.

[
52
]

Furthermore, the Court orders that the payments
for medical and dental expenses be managed and paid by Plaintiff directly with
the service provider and that receipts be remitted to him for insurance claim
purposes. Defendant will have to refund Plaintiff for the portion of the
medical and dental expenses not covered and considered as special expenses in
proportion of her earnings.

School fees

[
53
]

Defendant claims the following:

-           School uniform:                                   $522.13

-           School registration fees

at [school A]:                                         $300.00
[9]

-           School registration fees

at [school B] :                                        $250.00

-           School supplies:                                    $81.03
[10]

-           Hebrew program:
$400.00
[11]

Total:                                                        $1,553.16

[
54
]

In support of her claim, Defendant filed
invoices for part of the uniform expenses ($482.90) and for the registration
fees at [school B] ($250). She also filed proof of payment for the school
supplies ($81.03).

[
55
]

Plaintiff refuses to pay for the registration
fees at [school B] since he objected to registering X to this school as it is a
religious Jewish school. He claims that Defendant proceeded with the
registration despite his opposition. Additionally, he claims that this
registration fee is refundable with the exception of a $50 administration fee.

[
56
]

Defendant claims that she consulted Plaintiff
before registering X to [school B]. She also claims that Plaintiff agreed with
this school at first but later changed his mind. She adds that, due to
Plaintiff’s actions, she was no longer eligible for a refund.

[
57
]

Plaintiff also refuses to pay for the Hebrew
Studies P.E.L.O. program since it relates to teaching the child about Judaism
and Hebrew culture. He has repeatedly voiced his opposition to religious education
in a school setting.  Despite this, he claims that Defendant unilaterally
decided to enroll X in such a program for the past three years. He adds that,
in July 2016, Defendant accepted that X be enrolled in the Language Arts
Enrichment program. Once Plaintiff paid for this program, Defendant switched
the child to the Hebrew Studies P.E.L.O. program without consulting Plaintiff
and advised the school to apply the payment made towards the latter program.

[
58
]

Defendant states that Plaintiff agreed that X
could follow Hebrew classes as long as he did not have to pay for it. She adds
that the Hebrew Studies P.E.L.O. program is not a religious but rather a
language skills program.  She filed a letter sent by the program to the parents
in September 2015 explaining the changes made following a request from the
Ministère
de l’Éducation et de l’Enseignement Supérieur
to remove religious education
from the program curriculum. She adds that X is surrounded with friends and
family members that speaks Hebrew and that he expressed the desire to continue
learning the Hebrew language.

[
59
]

The Court dismisses Defendant’s claim for [school
A] registration fees, [school B] registration fees and school supplies as these
expenses fall within the basic parental contribution
and should not be considered as special expenses.
[12]

[
60
]

The Court grants Defendant’s claim for school
uniform since both parents agreed to register their child at a school where a
uniform is mandatory. Since these expenses occurred in 2014, Plaintiff must
reimburse 95% of the proven expenses, namely $458.75 ($482.90 x 95%).

[
61
]

The Court grants Defendant’s claim for the
Hebrew Studies P.E.L.O. program since the fees are not excessive and Hebrew
language is part of X’ culture. Since these expenses occurred in 2014 and 2015,
Plaintiff must reimburse 95% of the expense for 2014 ($200 x 95% = $190) and
76% of the expense for 2015 ($200 x 76%= $152).

Camp fees

[
62
]

Defendant claims an amount of $2,080 for eight
weeks of camp in 2015 and $885 for four weeks of camp in 2016.

[
63
]

Plaintiff states that the parties never agreed on
summer camps due to the unreasonable cost of the camps selected by Defendant
and her refusal to send X to less expensive local camps. Furthermore, he claims
that Defendant received a tax credit of $2,080 in 2015 relating to camp fees.
As for 2016, he states that he should not be obligated to incur any special
expense for camp fees since Defendant was not working. He
asks the Court to set a maximum amount payable for summer camps and to issue an
order for him to pay directly the service providers and to obtain the related
tax receipts.

[
64
]

Defendant has no issue with the camp invoices being
made to Plaintiff’s name. She is also prepared to forego claiming said expenses
in her tax returns as long as Plaintiff reimburses the camp fees.

[
65
]

The Court will not set a maximum amount payable
for summer camps in the future as these special
expenses must be reasonable in light of the revenues of both parties and relate
to the child’s particular needs.

[
66
]

The Court takes into consideration the fact that,
in 2015, Defendant received a tax credit for the entire amount relating to camp
fees and that, in 2016, she was not working. Therefore, the Court concludes
that Plaintiff must reimburse to Defendant an amount of $600 to cover summer
camp expenses occurred in 2015 and 2016.

Activities

[
67
]

Defendant claims the following activities fees:

2014

-           Judo lessons:                                     $270.00

-           Hip Hop lessons:                                 $45.00

Sub-total:                                                         $315.00

2015

-

Swimming lessons:                           $416.00

Sub-total:                                                         $416.00

2016

-          Guitar lessons:                                   $410.00

-          Ski lessons and equipment:            $575.05

Sub-total:                                                        $985.05

Total:
$1,716.05

[
68
]

Plaintiff states that Defendant purchased the
ski equipment and the lessons as a Hanouka present for X without consulting him
first. Furthermore, she did not offer to provide the equipment to Plaintiff as
to allow him to bring the child to perform this activity. As for the other
activities, he claims that Defendant selected them unilaterally too. He asks the Court to set a maximum amount payable for activities per
school semester and to issue an order for him to pay directly the service
providers and for him to obtain the related tax receipts.

[
69
]

Defendant has no issue with the invoices
regarding activities being issued to Plaintiff’s name and is prepared to forego
claiming said expenses in her tax returns as long as Plaintiff reimburses the activity
fees.

[
70
]

Plaintiff also requests that Defendant be
required, in the future, to pay her share of the special expenses based on her
income within 30 days of becoming employed. Defendant agrees with this request.

[
71
]

The Court will not set a maximum amount payable
for activities in the future as these special expenses must be reasonable in
light of the revenues of both parties and relate to the child’s particular
needs.

[
72
]

The Court considers that the activities expenses
for 2014 and 2015 fall within the basic parental contribution and should not be
considered as special expenses since the amounts claimed are less or equivalent
to 5% of the annual child support amount paid by Plaintiff which generally
relates to leisure expenses.
[13]

[
73
]

As for the activities expenses claimed for 2016, an amount of $348.71
representing 5% of the annual child support paid by Plaintiff in 2016 ($581.18
per month x 12 = $6 974.16 x 5% = $348.71) must be first deducted.

[
74
]

Even if Defendant did not consult Plaintiff, the
Court grants Defendant’s claim for the balance of the activities expenses in
2016 amounting to $636.34 ($985.05 - $348.71 = $636.34) since these fees are
not excessive in light of the revenues of both parties. However, in the future,
if Defendant disburses important activities fees without the consent of
Plaintiff, she may have to support the consequence of her choices.

[
75
]

In light of the above, the Court cannot issue
the requested orders regarding the payments of the activities to the service
providers and tax receipts.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
76
]

DECLARES
that
both parties will jointly exercise parental authority over their child and
ORDERS

them to consult one another before making any important decision regarding the
child, particularly concerning his health and education;

[
77
]

GRANTS
shared
custody to the parents as follows:

a)

X will be with each parent on a one-week
alternating basis;

b)

winter holidays will be split in two, one week
with each parent;

c)

spring break vacation will be split in two. The
parent not being able to take time off work will offer to the other parent the
opportunity to have custody during the day;

d)

X will be with Defendant for all important
Jewish holidays (Passover, Shavuot, Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippour, Sukkot, Simchat
Torah, and Hanouka
)
and if these holidays fall on Plaintiff’s time, the parties shall
exchange those days, when possible;

e)

X will be with Plaintiff on Christmas Eve and
Easter unless the parties agree otherwise;

f)

X will spend the day with Defendant on her
birthday and Mother’s Day and with Plaintiff on his birthday and Father’s Day;

g)

X will spend his birthday with Defendant on odd
years and with Plaintiff on even years;

h)

each parent shall have the child for a maximum
of two non-consecutive weeks of vacation time per year, unless both parents
agree to a longer period. Vacation schedules shall not interfere with the
rotating schedule which will be picked up where it ended before each break;

i)

the parties shall have to sign all documents
necessary to enable the minor child to leave Canada with the other parent for a
vacation provided there is mutual consent. The travelling parent shall give an
advance written notice 15 days before each vacation to the other parent with
the full disclosure of the itinerary and provide the other parent with easy
access to the child by phone during the vacation period; the child shall be
accompanied either by a parent or by an adult that the child is familiar with
and who has been agreed upon by both parents.

[
78
]

ORDERS
Plaintiff
to pay Defendant child support of $382.02 per month as of the date of this
judgment;

[
79
]

ORDERS
that the
child support be indexed on January 1
st
of each year;

[
80
]

DISMISSES

Defendant’s claim for vaccination fees;

[
81
]

ORDERS
that the
payments for medical and dental expenses be managed and paid by Plaintiff
directly with the service provider and that receipts be remitted to him for
insurance claim purposes;

[
82
]

ORDERS
that
Defendant reimburse Plaintiff for the portion of the medical and dental
expenses not covered and considered as special expenses in proportion of her
earnings;

[
83
]

ORDERS
Plaintiff
to pay to Defendant the following amounts as special expenses:

-

$347.00 for

Hebrew Studies P.E.L.O. program;

-

$458.75 for school uniform;

-          $600.00 for camp fees;

-          $636.34 for activities fees in 2016.

[
84
]

SUGGESTS
that the
parties

use an online co-parenting tool to
facilitate communication regarding X’ needs;

[
85
]

WITHOUT COSTS.
